Figure 1: Proposed pipeline combining blank/noise detection, CLIP-based domain routing, TC-LIA image– text alignment, and structured VLM outputs. An ensemble fuses these to pass the VLM response only for RELATED image–question pairs, while rejecting UNRELATED-REAL and BLANK/NOISE inputs to prevent mirage reasoning.

Figure 21: Per-layer RAPT curves for Gemma-3-4B-IT across four input conditions. Left: Image RAPT by layer. Right: Question RAPT by layer. The dotted vertical line marks the early/late split at layer 17. In the image RAPT panel, the unrelated image condition (red) tracks closely with the matched condition (blue) across all layers, confirming that the decoder allocates similar image attention regardless of whether the image is semantically relevant. The blank image condition (orange) shows suppressed but non-zero image RAPT, while no question (green) produces spuriously high image RAPT in late layers. In the question RAPT panel, the no question condition collapses to zero as expected, while all other conditions remain indistinguishable from each other in late layers. Together, these curves show that RAPT tracks modality budget allocation but cannot separate related from unrelated inputs — motivating TC-LIA’s patch–text cosine alignment as the decisional signal.

Figure 35: XGBoost feature importance across all VLM families. IAS is consistently the top feature.

Figure 34: Per-domain AUROC for binary RELATED vs. UNRELATED-REAL detection using final_cos (ViT-H/14 global cosine) alone versus the full Internal Alignment Score (IAS). IAS matches or exceeds final_cos across all domains. The largest gains appear in infovqa and docvqa, where a single global embedding is a weaker discriminator than the layer-wise patch-level alignment summary captured by IAS.

(a) Mean top-k patch–text alignment across all domains, showing a stronger late-layer rise for RELATED pairs than for UNRELATED-REAL or BLANK/NOISE inputs. (b) IAS distributions, where related inputs shift toward higher scores and non-related inputs remain lower or intermediate.

Figure 22: SAM3-style prompt-conditioned grounding sanity check. Related examples may not always produce stable evidence regions, whereas unrelated and blank/noise cases can produce unstable grounding.

Figure 9: Per-domain TC-LIA layerwise alignment curves for all three input conditions. Each panel shows the mean top-k patch–text alignment across 32 ViT-H/14 layers for one of the five evaluation domains. Medical domains (chest_vqa, pathvqa) show the sharpest late-layer rise for related pairs and the flattest curves for unrelated inputs, consistent with the domain-specific nature of medical questions. Natural-image and document domains show a similar but less pronounced pattern, reflecting the greater lexical ambiguity between questions and distractors.
Figure 8: Structured deterministic prompt used for VLM evaluation.

Figure 20: ∆RAPTimage heatmap under attention knockout (signed-log scale, real inputs). Rows are knocked-out layers; columns are RAPT measurement layers. The dark-blue diagonal marks the local suppression at the intervened layer. The red upper-triangle shows forward compensation: downstream layers increase their image-attention allocation to recover the blocked signal. Early knockouts (rows 0–10) produce the widest and strongest compensation because more downstream layers are available to redistribute attention.

Figure 7: Answer quality of the VLM backbones (BLEU, ROUGE-L, BERTScore F1). RELATED: scored against ground-truth. UNRELATED & BLANK: scored against six reference refusal phrases. Detailed percondition breakdown in Appendix K.

Despite having no relevant visual evidence, the base-prompt VLM confidently produces the identical answer “pituitary gland” for all three conditions; the ensemble correctly identifies each case.

Figure 27: Qualitative result cards for all three input conditions (RELATED, UNRELATED-REAL, BLANK/NOISE) on the same medical question (Aya-Vision-32B, chest_vqa, sample 17). The base-prompt VLM generates confident diagnoses (lymph nodes, calcifications) even for unrelated and blank inputs; the ensemble correctly identifies all three conditions.

Figure 15: Text-conditioned GradCAM maps across three input conditions (columns: related, unrelatedreal, blank). For unrelated inputs, GradCAM fires on spurious visually salient regions that bear no relation to the question. For blank inputs, activations are near-uniform or randomly scattered. GradCAM cannot separate related from unrelated inputs (AUROC 0.543), motivating the move to patch–text cosine alignment in TC-LIA.

Figure 13: Left: 3-class accuracy on the held-out domain. Right: Mirage rate on the held-out domain. ChestVQA is the most challenging held-out domain (MR = 6.7%); InfoVQA is the easiest (MR = 1.4%, Acc = 96.3%).

Table 2: TC-LIA feature comparison for llava-onevision-qwen2-7b-si-hf. IAS produces the strongest composite scalar relevance score.
Figure 23: Qualitative result cards for all three input conditions (Related, Unrelated-Real, Blank/Noise) on the same question using Gemma-3-4B-IT.

Figure 19: RAPTimage cascade under single-layer knockout (real inputs). Each line shows the change in image-attention RAPT relative to baseline when layer k is knocked out (k ∈ {0, 8, 17, 25, 33}). The knocked-out layer shows a sharp local drop (diagonal dip), but all other observed layers return to near-zero deviation, confirming that the network compensates for the blocked layer by redistributing image attention downstream. Visual grounding in Gemma-3-4B-IT is therefore distributed and cannot be suppressed by a single-layer intervention.

Figure 10: Per-domain distributions of the TC-LIA Internal Alignment Score (IAS) across the three input conditions. Each panel shows the IAS histogram for one evaluation domain. RELATED image–question pairs generally shift toward higher IAS values, while UNRELATED-REAL examples concentrate at lower scores and BLANK/NOISE examples form a narrower intermediate distribution. These domain-wise patterns show that TC-LIA provides discriminative pre-generation evidence for separating answerable inputs from mirage-prone cases.

Figure 2: TC-LIA computes text-conditioned layer-wise patch alignment from CLIP ViT-H/14 features. Latelayer top-k alignment, alignment gain, slope, final cosine similarity, and IAS are used as mirage detection features.
